assumptions: The initial payer is a Polish accounting or AP software platform with a portfolio large enough for one integration to create meaningful activated usage, rather than individual SMEs.
The base product remains useful through VAT-registry evidence, change freezes, secure supplier remediation, dual approval and audit packets even when the host cannot supply a reusable VoP response.
VoP evidence is accepted only through interfaces and contractual rights already held by the host; the business does not depend on direct EPC access or on charging for the legally free VoP check.

A registry-first sandbox integration can be built within roughly PLN 50,000 and 12-18 founder hours per week using AI and limited contractors, while production security and certification work is deferred until an economically testable pilot.
No partner commitment, price acceptance, activation volume, data right, renewal rate, implementation cost or liability cost is assumed to exist until demonstrated.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The concept correctly identifies that the monetizable layer is not a free name/IBAN result but the supplier-change control, remediation and audit workflow around it. Embedding at a host platform's change and payment gate also combines access and portfolio distribution in one relationship. The insight is coherent, though established verification vendors already pursue adjacent workflow positions.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Supplier impersonation and fraudulent bank-detail changes are documented, consequential problems, and paid incumbents show that organizations buy account-validation and master-data controls. However, the redesigned payer is the software host, not necessarily the business bearing the fraud loss, and there is no evidence that a Polish host will pay rather than build, rely on bank controls or pass the cost through.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: An OEM minimum plus portfolio- or usage-linked fees could produce recurring, high-leverage revenue because acquisition and integration are amortized across many managed entities. That structure is attractive in principle, but contract value, revenue share, activation, retention, sales-cycle cost, implementation effort, exception operations, security, hosting and liability are all unknown. Early partner-specific work could absorb margin and founder capacity before volume appears.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Polish accounting and AP platforms are a focused beachhead with a clear trigger and buyer, and a single sufficiently large portfolio could be economically meaningful. The supplied evidence does not establish the number and concentration of reachable hosts, their managed-company volumes, qualifying event frequency or a beachhead revenue pool large enough to support the founder-wealth objective.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Deep placement at a host's supplier-master and payment gate could create a strong position inside that installed portfolio. Yet SurePay, Trustpair, banks and ERP or platform teams can cover overlapping controls, the official registry is free, and the host owns the customer relationship and can build or replace the module. No exclusive integration, proprietary access or superior outcome is established.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A successful Polish host deployment could extend to other accounting and AP platforms, outsourced finance operators, supplier onboarding, change monitoring, anomaly detection and selected CEE or EU markets. Expansion is plausible but each new host or geography may require new integrations, registries, language handling, data-rights analysis and enterprise procurement.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Integration depth, accumulated resolution rules, auditable history and workflow switching costs could compound after adoption. Those advantages depend on contractual rights to retain and reuse data and may remain host-specific; the host controls distribution and may own much of the resulting data. The underlying checks and workflow components are copyable, and established vendors already possess integrations and trust.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: A Poland-specific, white-label control that operates in the host's existing workflow could be more convenient than a separate portal and can add remediation and auditability beyond a free registry lookup. There is no measured reduction in fraud, manual work, false matches or implementation burden, and no evidence that the offer is decisively better than incumbent, bank or internally built alternatives.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Recognized BEC risk and Poland's approaching 2027 VoP timetable create attention and a concrete integration window. The same regulation makes the bank-provided check free and encourages banks and incumbents to improve their own flows, so timing creates both demand for surrounding controls and substitution pressure on the proposed module.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: One design-partner integration can reach many managed companies and is compatible with the founder's preference for concentrated, low-volume selling. However, the first platform is the sole initial route to market, no partner has committed, and enterprise procurement, security review and integration create a potentially long, relationship-intensive sales motion. Repeatability across hosts is unproven.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: Entity resolution, anomaly logic, evidence packaging and SDK development fit the founder's skills, and a non-custodial prototype is feasible part-time with AI leverage. Production demands tenant isolation, lawful data handling, security review, reliable matching, careful assurance language, professional liability management and platform integration. These can be staged, but the partner-dependent workload could exceed the founder's time and capital before commercial proof.

main_structural_strength: A single host integration can place the control at the exact supplier-change gate and distribute it across a managed-company portfolio, coupling workflow access, recurring usage and lower per-entity acquisition effort without assuming direct EPC access.
primary_score_limiter: The first platform contract is simultaneously the buyer, distribution channel, integration surface and source of any lawful VoP evidence, while willingness to pay, activation, implementation burden, margins and renewal are all unresolved.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: The core VoP check must be free to payment-service users and is not generically available to an independent AP application, while established vendors already sell overlapping verification, onboarding and audit workflows; this removes commodity-check pricing power and makes host adoption depend on differentiated surrounding workflow value.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A paid or contractually priced pilot with a named Polish accounting or AP platform that specifies integration and data rights, demonstrates the registry-and-remediation workflow remains valuable without reusable VoP access, and measures activated entities, supplier-change volume, exception labor, implementation cost, gross margin, sales-cycle effort, renewal intent and loss-or-work reduction.
highest_value_structural_change: Make the product contractually and technically VoP-optional: sell a self-contained supplier-change freeze, registry, secure remediation and dual-approval control with a standard optional host VoP adapter, so distribution and workflow value no longer fail if a host lacks rights to expose or retain the bank response.
